Q: Java Sequential UUID A:

tl;dr

No need to invent a new kind of identifier.

The UUID standard expanded to invent new index-friendly kinds of UUID.

  • Use Version 7 UUID for new tables or for greenfield projects.
  • Consider migrating to Version 6 UUIDs in existing tables using Version 1 UUIDs.

Use a database engine sophisticated enough to support UUID as a native type.

In Java:

UUID.ofEpochMillis( Instant.now().toEpochMilli() )

UUID is not text

Understand that a UUID consists of exactly 128 bits, not text, not characters. But humans do not do well with reading or writing one hundred and twenty eight 0 & 1 digits. So for human consumption, we present UUID values in a more compact textual form.

Using a VARCHAR(36) column

I presume you meant 36 characters because the canonical representation of a UUID is done with 32 hexadecimal characters grouped with a hyphen as four delimiters. For example:

019de0e9-c62b-7ce7-9304-404168bd4a89

But, no, do not do this. Do not store UUID as text. Doing so would be grossly wasteful of storage and RAM. ASCII and UTF-8 encodings would use 8 bits * 36 characters = 288 bits. UTF-16 would double that to 576 bits. That is more than double and quadruple the 128 bits actually contained in a UUID.

A more sophisticated database engine will provide support for UUID as a native data type. For example, Postgres offers a UUID type.

This means a UUID column will store exactly the 128 bits that makes up a UUID. No text, no characters, just bits. This saves on space written to storage, and saves memory when loading rows. Additionally, space is saved when building an index.

Avoid indexing random/unordered data

java's version 4 UUID random generator

No, do not use Version 4 UUID values, if at all possible.

With Version 4, 122 of the 128 bits in a UUID value is entirely random. Such random values do not provide for efficient indexing.

but the problem with it is that the UUIDs aren't sequential

I will assume you meant “ordered” rather than strictly “sequential” (which means a series of numbers without omission such as 1, 2, 3, 4, …). And I will assume that your expressed concern involves that inefficient indexing I mentioned above.

Your concern is well-founded. On larger tables, indexing random or unordered Version 1 through Version 5 UUIDs does become inefficient enough to cause measurable performance problems.

New index-friendly UUID Versions

Good news! We now have index-friendly UUIDs.

In 2024-05, the specification for UUID was dramatically revamped, with RFC 9562 obsoleting RFC 4122. Two new Versions of UUID were invented to avoid the problems of inefficient indexing.

  • Version 6 is a reworking of Version 1.
    • Same bits, different layout arrangement (except of course for the four bits of Version number).
    • Brownfield systems currently using Version 1 UUIDs should consider migrating to Version 6 if needing a performance boost. UUID values can be converted between Version 1 and Version 6, back and forth, without data loss.
  • Version 7 in entirely new.
    • Version 7 is based on a point in time like Versions 1 & 6, but using the more common epoch reference seen in UNIX-like systems and elsewhere: 1970-01-01T00:00Z. The granularity of time is milliseconds rather than the unusual 100-microseconds. Most importantly, the bits of the timestamp are arranged in most-significant order, unlike Version 1, with a 48-bit big-endian unsigned number for the efficient indexing we seek. Sub-millisecond resolution is optional.
    • Unlike Version 1, Version 7 is not based on a point in space. For privacy and network-security, the MAC address (or other node identifier) used in Version 1 is replaced with random bits.
    • Furthermore, 12 bits are available to optionally provide additional monotonicity.

Version 7 is generally recommended as your first consideration when choosing to use UUID values.

You said:

My idea would basically be the same, generate a UUID using UUID.randomUUID() and then replace the MSB from the resulting id with System.currentTimeMillis().

You basically described Version 7 UUID: Time-based, with a Unix-style and Java-style epoch reference of first moment of 1970 in UTC, as a count of milliseconds (or finer), with most significant bits first, combined with some random bits, providing for monotonic ordered UUIDs even when created across various systems independently.

Java

The existing java.util.UUID class is compatible with Version 6 and Version 7. Ironically that is because the implementation of that class did not validate the bits. So the new bit values identifying the new Versions 6, 7, and 8 are inadvertently accepted by the java.util.UUID class.

The catch is generating values. For that, a new feature arrived in Java 26. Call the new method UUID.ofEpochMillis. Pass a count of milliseconds.

UUID uuid = UUID.ofEpochMillis( Instant.now().toEpochMilli() );

That code is a bit annoying, so you may want to write a little static factory method.

public static UUID uuid7() {
    return UUID.ofEpochMillis( Instant.now().toEpochMilli() );
}

For earlier versions of Java, or to access the optional features of Version 7 UUID, use one of the multiple libraries available in the Java ecosystem.

Q: How to transfer installed packages from an older version of R in the newest one A:

This might do what you want.

inst_pack <- function(x, lib = .libPaths()[1], ncpus = 1L){
  utils::install.packages(
    pkgs = x,
    lib = lib,
    repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org",
    Ncpus = ncpus
  )
}

## Default repo
local({r <- getOption("repos")
r["CRAN"] <- "https://cran.r-project.org" 
options(repos=r)
})

#
inst_pkgs <- installed.packages(priority = "NA")
inst_pkgname <- inst_pkgs[, "Package"]
inst_version <- inst_pkgs[, "Version"] |> package_version()
#
avail_pkgs <- available.packages(repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
avail_pkgname <- avail_pkgs[, "Package"]
avail_version <- avail_pkgs[, "Version"] |> package_version()

i <- which(avail_pkgname %in% inst_pkgname)
j <- which(inst_pkgname %in% avail_pkgname)

sum(avail_version[i] > inst_version[j])
i_update <- which(avail_version[i] > inst_version[j])

ncores <- 1L
# with so many packages to update, it might be a good idea
# to use this instead of 'ncores <- 1L'
# ncores <- parallel::detectCores() - 2L
to_update <- avail_pkgname[i][i_update]
inst_pack(to_update, ncpus = ncores)

When I ran this I got the following message.

  There are binary versions available but the source versions are later:
           binary source needs_compilation
devtools    2.5.1  2.5.2             FALSE
fabletools  0.6.1  0.7.0             FALSE
roxygen2    7.3.3  8.0.0              TRUE
secretbase  1.2.1  1.2.2              TRUE

And those packages' latest versions were installed from source.

Q: TWRP: Unable to mount storage; Internal Storage (0MB); Install process fails A:

Note : This will wipe/format your Data portion and your data will be reset.

INSTRUCTIONS :

  1. Reboot your device into TWRP Recovery.

  2. Go to Wipe menu.

  3. Go to Advance Wipe.

  4. Select Data and go to Repair or Change File System.

  5. Click Repair File System. (If not fix, go to step number 6)

  6. Go to Change File System.

  7. Select Ext2 and swipe to confirm.

  8. Now change back to Ext4 and swipe to confirm.

  9. Now go back and check if your portions can be mount or not from Mount menu.

  10. If not fix, repair your Internal partition. (This may wipe your Internal storage).

OR Unlock your boot loader again

Q: Caught exception during boot: org.jboss.as.controller.persistence.ConfigurationPersistenceException: WFLYCTL0085: Failed to parse configuration A:

In my case the standalone.xml file located in wildfly-10.1.0.Final\standalone\configuration was completely blank, luckily, I had a backup.

I copied everything to the standalone.xml file and the problem was solved, wildfly was able to run smoothly again.

Q: getting the position from the png image of LUDO game A:

I assume you want to set the pieces on the ludo board image to show the user's progress throughout the game.

The way you are doing that it can be done by managing the aspect ratio and placing the pieces accordingly, which is quite tough, and can't predict if it will actually work or not. If you want to use naive android, use a 15x15 grid and break the image accordingly. Later use the grid positions as co-ordinate for your colored pieces.

If you are searching for easier options, use Game Engines like Unity, but it may create a larger size APK file for your game.

Q: Expected linebreaks to be 'LF' but found 'CRLF' linebreak-style A:

I know this is an old thread but I want to bump it because I have a solution that works for me

First turn off git automatic line-end conversion, run this command:

git config --global core.autocrlf false

Force all text files to use LF line endings, create .gitattributes on your project's root folder. Copy and paste this:

* text=auto eol=lf

Untrack all files, run:

git rm --cached -r .

Re-checks all files from last commit, apply the rules everywhere, run:

git reset --hard

done!
